title: Given a `List<Employee>`, collect them into a `Map<Long, String>` of id to name that preserves the original insertion order, by supplying `LinkedHashMap::new` as the map supplier to `Collectors.toMap`.
shortTitle: Collect employees into a LinkedHashMap preserving insertion order using Collectors.toMap with a map supplier
keyPoints: The default `Collectors.toMap` returns a `HashMap`, which gives no guarantee about iteration order.
The four-argument `toMap(key, value, merge, supplier)` lets you choose the concrete map type via a supplier.
Passing `LinkedHashMap::new` makes the result iterate in the order elements arrived in the stream.
The four-argument overload forces you to also provide a merge function, even if duplicates are not expected.
`LinkedHashMap` preserves insertion order because it links entries in a doubly linked list alongside the hash table.
Use `TreeMap::new` instead when you want keys sorted rather than kept in insertion order.

s1_definition.oneliner: `toMap(Employee::getId, Employee::getName, (a, b) -> a, LinkedHashMap::new)` builds an id-to-name map whose iteration order matches the order the employees appeared in the stream.
s1_definition.profdef:
The four-argument `Collectors.toMap` controls the concrete `Map` implementation.

- **Key mapper** – extracts the key, here `Employee::getId`.
- **Value mapper** – extracts the value, here `Employee::getName`.
- **Merge function** – a `BinaryOperator` required by this overload; it resolves duplicate keys.
- **Map supplier** – a factory such as `LinkedHashMap::new` that decides which `Map` type holds the result.

The default two-argument form uses a `HashMap`, so iteration order is unspecified. Supplying `LinkedHashMap::new` keeps entries in the order they were inserted.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, Rajesh records new account openings in a ledger. A plain `HashMap` is like tossing the slips into a drawer: they are all there, but when you reopen the drawer they come out in an unpredictable jumble. A `LinkedHashMap` is like a bound ledger book where each new account is written on the next line, so reading the book back always follows the order accounts were opened. The map supplier is Rajesh choosing the bound ledger instead of the loose drawer.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  List<Employee>: [ (30,Rajesh), (10,Priya), (20,Pankaj) ]
        │
        │  toMap(getId, getName, merge, SUPPLIER)
        ▼
   choose SUPPLIER
        │
   ┌────┴───────────────┬──────────────────────┐
   ▼                    ▼                        ▼
 HashMap::new      LinkedHashMap::new        TreeMap::new
 (default)         (insertion order)         (sorted keys)
   │                    │                        │
   ▼                    ▼                        ▼
 {20=Pankaj,       {30=Rajesh,              {10=Priya,
  10=Priya,         10=Priya,                20=Pankaj,
  30=Rajesh}        20=Pankaj}               30=Rajesh}
 unspecified        source order             key order
```

```text
  LinkedHashMap entry layout
  ┌──────────── hash buckets (fast lookup) ────────────┐
  │ bucket[a] -> (30,Rajesh)                            │
  │ bucket[b] -> (10,Priya)                             │
  │ bucket[c] -> (20,Pankaj)                            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │ also linked in insertion order
            ▼
  head -> (30,Rajesh) -> (10,Priya) -> (20,Pankaj) -> tail
         iteration follows this chain
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When Rajesh collects employees into a `Map<Long, String>`, the quick two-argument `Collectors.toMap` gives him a `HashMap`. Everything is in there, but the iteration order is unpredictable, the way loose slips tossed in a drawer come out jumbled. For a statement or ledger where the reader expects the same order the accounts were opened, that is not good enough.

The fix is the four-argument overload. You keep the same key mapper `Employee::getId` and value mapper `Employee::getName`, add a merge function to satisfy the overload, and pass `LinkedHashMap::new` as the map supplier. Now the result iterates in the exact order the employees appeared in the stream, like reading entries down the lines of a bound ledger.

`LinkedHashMap` achieves this by keeping a doubly linked list of entries alongside the usual hash buckets. Lookups stay fast because they still use the buckets, while iteration follows the linked list, which records insertion order. If you need sorted keys instead of arrival order, swap the supplier for `TreeMap::new`.

Two details trip people up. The supplier overload makes the merge function mandatory, so you must supply something like `(a, b) -> a` even when duplicates are not expected. And when a duplicate key does occur, the merge updates the value but the key stays in its original position.

In our banking work the rule is to pick the map type on purpose: default `HashMap` when order does not matter, `LinkedHashMap` to mirror the source, and `TreeMap` to sort.

Remember one sentence: pass `LinkedHashMap::new` as the fourth argument to `toMap` to keep entries in the order the stream produced them.
